whyThisMatters: Real Technology Team moments are fast — a ticket, a call, an alert, a PR, a dependency, a CI notification — and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits across the full range of what the job throws at you, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a plausible ticket number, a familiar tool's look, a caller who won't wait, a package with the right name, a PR comment that reads like a real review. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. With the combined pool now covering both help-desk and development scenarios, most people get at least one from the "other side" wrong on their first try.
Ask why asking a caller for a ticket reference number, or a contributor for more details, doesn't actually verify anything in either case.
Ask why taking extra time despite pressure is listed as a good habit, even when it feels like it's making someone else's problem worse.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to verify a request that already looks like a normal part of their job.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like part of the job — a plausible ticket number, a tool's familiar look, an urgent caller, a package with a reasonable name, a PR comment styled like a real review — without checking the actual sending domain, console, or publish history. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit, on either side of the combined set.

bubbles.text: Check the ticket in the real queue
bubbles.why: If a ticket isn't in the real queue, the request is likely a scam.

bubbles.text: Trust a ticket number alone
bubbles.why: Attackers can guess or quote ticket numbers; it doesn't prove who is calling.

bubbles.text: Verify callers on the approved list
bubbles.why: Checking the approved list exposes impostors pretending to be staff.

bubbles.text: Give remote access to a caller
bubbles.why: Remote access lets an attacker take control of your computer and data.

bubbles.text: Refuse to skip identity checks
bubbles.why: Identity checks stop attackers who pressure you into helping them.

bubbles.text: Reset a password without checking ID
bubbles.why: Unverified resets let attackers take over someone else's account.

bubbles.text: Read a one-time code to a caller
bubbles.why: One-time codes are the last lock on an account; sharing one opens it.

bubbles.text: Check MDM profile permissions
bubbles.why: Reviewing permissions shows if a profile would give someone control of the device.

bubbles.text: Install an MDM profile unread
bubbles.why: A rogue profile can give attackers control over your device and data.

bubbles.text: Confirm DLP exceptions in the system
bubbles.why: The official record proves an exception is real, not just claimed in an email.

bubbles.text: Approve a DLP exception by email
bubbles.why: Emails are easily faked, so approving this way can leak sensitive data.

bubbles.text: Open GitHub directly, not via links
bubbles.why: Typing the address avoids fake login pages that steal your account.

bubbles.text: Click a re-authorize link in a PR
bubbles.why: Fake re-authorize links hand attackers access to your code account.

bubbles.text: Check the CI dashboard directly
bubbles.why: Going straight to the dashboard avoids fake build alerts that steal logins.

bubbles.text: Re-enter a Git token from an email link
bubbles.why: A token typed into a fake page lets attackers access your code.

bubbles.text: Verify recruiters independently
bubbles.why: Fake recruiters use job offers to get you to run harmful code or share data.

bubbles.text: Run a script from a stranger's message
bubbles.why: Unrequested scripts can install malware that steals credentials and files.

bubbles.text: Check an app's publisher first
bubbles.why: Rogue apps pose as real ones to gain access to your accounts.

bubbles.text: Give admin access to an unknown app
bubbles.why: An unknown app with admin rights can read or change all your company data.

bubbles.text: Update extensions via the marketplace
bubbles.why: Genuine updates come from the official store; fake ones can carry malware.

bubbles.text: Install an extension from a link
bubbles.why: Extensions from outside the marketplace can secretly steal data.

bubbles.text: Rotate secrets in the vault, not email
bubbles.why: Emailed secrets can be read by anyone who gets into the mailbox.

bubbles.text: Email .env values in reply
bubbles.why: Environment files hold keys and passwords that attackers can reuse.

bubbles.text: Count a ticket number as verification
bubbles.why: A caller can quote or invent a ticket number, so it doesn't prove identity.

bubbles.text: Treat a routine reset as proof
bubbles.why: A reset request that looks routine can still be an attacker's setup.
